newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German chemical industry more confident.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German chemical industry more confident.

text.p: The German chemical industry, suffering at the hands of recent price declines which helped dent first-half sales, is more confident for the second half as domestic demand is forecast to pick up again.

Reporting on the first half of the year, the German chemical industry association VCI said on Wednesday that first- half sales slipped around 5.5 percent while prices eased 3.3 percent from year-ago levels.
For the year as a whole VCI President Juergen Strube forecast total production would be one percent above 1995 levels while sales would still be one percent below year-ago levels.

Strube, also management board chairman at BASF AG one of Germany's leading chemical companies, said "companies expect livelier domestic demand in the second half, as well as ongoing good sales abroad."
Already in the first half, Strube said that data for the chemical industry showed the industry's strong international orientation as "the right way".

German companies reported a 2.1 percent rise in exports to North and Central America during the first half but a 10.9 percent drop in exports to South America. Exports to Asia, where German companies are very keen to expand their presence, dropped 2.7 percent.
In total, Strube said first-half 1996 chemical sales were around 89 billion marks ($60.16 billion) with exports totalling 52 billion marks, marking a one percent increase from year-ago levels.
Domestic sales dropped around 7.8 percent while foreign sales eased about one percent.
Meanwhile imports dropped by two percent to around 31 billion marks. Due to the reduced domestic sales the import quota, however, rose to 45 percent.
Plaguing the industry most during the first half was soft domestic demand which Strube said was "weak and clearly below year-ago levels" during the first half of 1996.

Consequently production dropped by around 3.5 percent, with inorganic basic chemicals and plastics taking the biggest hit. On the other hand, production in agricultural chemical and pharmaceuticals continued to grow.
For the year, Strube said pharmaceutical production should show a rise between two and three percent.
As economies recover around the world, Strube predicted the decline in prices would come to and end soon, adding "and we will see a small rise in prices" in coming months.

To improve Germany's status as a production site, Strube, echoing many industrialists' calls, urged the German government to simplify processes regulating foreign investments and overhaul the complicated tax system.

"We want to conduct research and work here sucessfully in the future," Strube said, adding the government also needed to continue forging ahead in paving the way for companies to do more work in the biotechnology area.

German legislation governing biotechnological research and production, reflecting Germans' fears about the subject following World War Two, has been very restrictive and has thus allowed other nations to establish a sizable lead over Germany.

Strube said the chemical industry would benefit from a common European currency, particularly since much trade is still conducted in Europe, and he urged nations to keep working on getting budgets into shape to join the currency union.
